translation: Though He rides a fierce battle-ready bull and performs the deed of dissolving all the worlds, though He wears aathi flowers in His matted hair and destroys the desires of those who reach Him, and though His shoulders bear garlands and He is a great ascetic and a sage of penance, O friend with dark cloud-like tresses, I will never cease my love for him even in a dream.
commentary: To love God is to surrender to the very force that dissolves the universe and destroys all personal desires. The heroine knows her Lord is a fierce ascetic whose cosmic role is to bring all things to an end. She welcomes this absolute destruction, realizing that losing her worldly desires is the only way to be united with him completely.

tamil: கோதே மருவார் மால்அயனும் குறியா நெறியார் என்றாலும்
சாதே மகிழ்வார் அடியாரைத் தம்போல் நினைப்பார் என்றாலும்
மாதே வருக்கும் மாதேவர் மௌன யோகி என்றாலும்
காதேர் குழையாய் நான்அவர்மேல் காதல் ஒழியேன் கனவினுமே.
translit: kōtē maruvār mālayaṉum kuṟiyā neṟiyār eṉṟālum cātē makiḻvār aṭiyārait tampōl niṉaippār eṉṟālum mātē varukkum mātēvar mauṉa yōki eṉṟālum kātēr kuḻaiyāy nāṉavarmēl kātal oḻiyēṉ kaṉaviṉumē.
translation: O friend with beautiful earrings! Even if He embraces no flaws, even if His path cannot be conceived by Vishnu and Brahma, even if He rejoices in the virtuous and considers His devotees equal to Himself, even if He is the supreme Lord to all great gods, and even if He is a silent yogi, I will never cease my love for him even in a dream.
commentary: The speaker addresses her friend to declare her unwavering devotion. She lists the Lord's supreme qualities: He is beyond the reach of the great creator and preserver gods, and He is the ultimate silent ascetic. A silent yogi might seem too distant for romantic love. Yet she insists that her deep affection for Him will never fade, even in her dreams.

tamil: உடையார் உலகிற் காசென்பார்க் கொன்றும் உதவார் ஆனாலும்
அடையார்க் கரியார் வேண்டார்க்கே அருள்வார் வலிய ஆனாலும்
படையார் கரத்தர் பழிக்கஞ்சாப் பாசு பதரே ஆனாலும்
கடையா அமுதே நான்அவர்மேல் காதல் ஒழியேன் கனவினுமே.
translit: uṭaiyār ulakiṟ kāceṉpārk koṉṟum utavār āṉālum aṭaiyārk kariyār vēṇṭārkkē aruḷvār valiya āṉālum paṭaiyār karattar paḻikkañcāp pācu patarē āṉālum kaṭaiyā amutē nāṉavarmēl kātal oḻiyēṉ kaṉaviṉumē.
translation: O unchurned ambrosia! Even if He possesses all things yet gives nothing to those in the world who beg for a coin, even if He remains rare to those who do not approach Him yet forcefully grants grace to the desireless, and even if He holds a weapon in His hand as the Lord of creatures who fears no blame, I will never cease my love for him even in a dream.
commentary: The Lord acts in ways that confuse ordinary people. He owns the entire universe but will not give a single coin to those who beg for worldly wealth. He gives his grace forcefully to those who desire nothing, while remaining hidden from those who do not truly seek him. He cares nothing for public opinion or blame. Despite his fierce and unpredictable nature, the speaker loves him completely.

note: Editor's note: theme (turai): the heroine speaks to her friend (tōḻiyoṭu kūṟal, தோழியொடு கூறல்).
tamil: ஓணம் உடையான் தொழுதேத்தும் ஒற்றி நகர்வாழ் உத்தமர்பால்
மாண வலியச் சென்றென்னை மருவி அணைவீர் என்றேநான்
நாணம் விடுத்து நவின்றாலும் நாமார் நீயார் என்பாரேல்
ஏண விழியாய் என்செய்வேன் என்னை மடவார் இகழாரோ.
translit: ōṇam uṭaiyāṉ toḻutēttum oṟṟi nakarvāḻ uttamarpāl māṇa valiyac ceṉṟeṉṉai maruvi aṇaivīr eṉṟēnāṉ nāṇam viṭuttu naviṉṟālum nāmār nīyār eṉpārēl ēṇa viḻiyāy eṉceyvēṉ eṉṉai maṭavār ikaḻārō.
translation: Even if I go resolutely to the supreme Lord living in Otri city, who is worshipped by Vishnu, and cast aside my modesty to say, "Embrace me and hold me," what if He replies, "Who are we, and who are you?" O friend with deer-like eyes, what will I do? Will not the women mock me?
commentary: The soul is ready to cast aside all worldly pride and conventional modesty to seek God directly. Speaking as a young woman deeply in love, the speaker fears the ultimate rejection. The terror is not just what society will say, but the devastating possibility that God might look at her and pretend not to know her.

tamil: காதம் மணக்குங் கடிமலர்ப்பூங் காவார் ஒற்றிக் கண்நுதலார்
போதம் மணக்கும் புனிதர்அவர் பொன்னம் புயத்தைப் புணரேனேல்
சீதம் மணக்குங் குழலாய்என் சிந்தை மயங்கித் தியங்குமடி
ஏதம் மணக்கும் என்செய்வேன் என்னை மடவார் இகழாரோ.
translit: kātam maṇakkuṅ kaṭimalarppūṅ kāvār oṟṟik kaṇnutalār pōtam maṇakkum puṉitaravar poṉṉam puyattaip puṇarēṉēl cītam maṇakkuṅ kuḻalāyeṉ cintai mayaṅkit tiyaṅkumaṭi ētam maṇakkum eṉceyvēṉ eṉṉai maṭavār ikaḻārō.
translation: The Lord with the eye on His forehead resides in Otri, surrounded by groves with fragrant blossoms smelling for leagues. He is the pure one redolent with wisdom. If I do not embrace His golden shoulders, O friend with cool fragrant hair, my mind will be confused and bewildered. Harm will surround me. What will I do? Will not the women mock me?
commentary: Separation from the divine brings absolute mental confusion. The speaker looks at the fragrant, beautiful world around her and feels only the danger of spiritual ruin if she cannot unite with God. Without the anchor of divine wisdom, the human mind simply falls apart.

tamil: பண்ணார் மொழியார் உருக்காட்டும் பணைசூழ் ஒற்றிப் பதியினர்என்
கண்ணார் மணிபோன் றென்உயிரில் கலந்து வாழும் கள்வர்அவர்
நண்ணார் இன்னும் திருஅனையாய் நான்சென் றிடினும் நலம்அருள
எண்ணார் ஆயின் என்செய்வேன் என்னை மடவார் இகழாரோ.
translit: paṇṇār moḻiyār urukkāṭṭum paṇaicūḻ oṟṟip patiyiṉareṉ kaṇṇār maṇipōṉ ṟeṉuyiril kalantu vāḻum kaḷvaravar naṇṇār iṉṉum tiru-aṉaiyāy nāṉceṉ ṟiṭiṉum nalamaruḷa eṇṇār āyiṉ eṉceyvēṉ eṉṉai maṭavār ikaḻārō.
translation: The Lord of Otri city is surrounded by fields where women with musical voices reveal their beauty. He is the thief who lives mingled in my life like the pupil of my eye. He still does not approach me, O friend like Lakshmi. Even if I go to Him, if He does not think to grant me joy, what will I do? Will not the women mock me?
commentary: God is intimately close, living within the soul like the pupil inside an eye. Yet to the agonizing speaker, He feels entirely absent and distant. This tension between God's deep inner presence and His outward silence causes unbearable pain.

tamil: ஊர்என் றுடையீர் ஒற்றிதனை உலக முடையீர் என்னைஅணை
வீர்என் றவர்முன் பலர்அறிய வெட்கம் விடுத்துக் கேட்டாலும்
சேர்என் றுரைத்தால் அன்றிஅவர் சிரித்துத் திருவாய் மலர்ந்தெனைநீ
யார்என் றுரைத்தால் என்செய்வேன் என்னை மடவார் இகழாரோ.
translit: ūreṉ ṟuṭaiyīr oṟṟitaṉai ulaka muṭaiyīr eṉṉai-aṇai vīreṉ ṟavarmuṉ palaraṟiya veṭkam viṭuttuk kēṭṭālum cēreṉ ṟuraittāl aṉṟi-avar cirittut tiruvāy malarnteṉainī yāreṉ ṟuraittāl eṉceyvēṉ eṉṉai maṭavār ikaḻārō.
translation: "You hold Otri as Your city, and You hold the world. Embrace me." Even if I cast aside shame and ask Him this in front of many people, what if He does not tell me to join Him? What if He smiles, opens His sacred lips, and asks me, "Who are you?" What will I do? Will not the women mock me?
commentary: True devotion often requires stepping outside of social norms and risking public ridicule. The soul imagines boldly demanding God's love in front of a crowd. The deepest fear remains that God might simply smile and ask who she is, leaving her completely exposed to the mocking world.

tamil: சோமன் நிலவுந் தூய்ச்சடையார் சொல்லிற் கலந்த சுவையானார்
சேமம் நிலவுந் திருஒற்றித் தேவர் இன்னும் சேர்ந்திலர்நான்
தாமம் அருள்வீர் என்கினும்இத் தருணத் திசையா தென்பாரேல்
ஏம முலையாய் என்செய்வேன் என்னை மடவார் இகழாரோ.
translit: cōmaṉ nilavun tūyccaṭaiyār colliṟ kalanta cuvaiyāṉār cēmam nilavun tiru-oṟṟit tēvar iṉṉum cērntilarnāṉ tāmam aruḷvīr eṉkiṉumit taruṇat ticaiyā teṉpārēl ēma mulaiyāy eṉceyvēṉ eṉṉai maṭavār ikaḻārō.
translation: He has pure matted hair where the moon shines. He has become the sweetness mingled in words. The Lord of sacred Otri, where safety prevails, has not yet joined me. Even if I say, "Grant me Your garland," what if He says, "I will not consent at this time"? O friend with golden breasts, what will I do? Will not the women mock me?
commentary: God is the very sweetness found in language and the ultimate source of safety. Even so, the divine timing is entirely His own. The soul constantly worries that God might delay their union simply because the moment is not yet right.

tamil: வில்லை மலையாய்க் கைக்கொண்டார் விடஞ்சூழ் கண்டர் விரிபொழில்சூழ்
தில்லை நகரார் ஒற்றியுளார் சேர்ந்தார் அல்லர் நான்அவர்பால்
ஒல்லை அடைந்து நின்றாலும் உன்னை அணைதல் ஒருபோதும்
இல்லை எனிலோ என்செய்கேன் என்னை மடவார் இகழாரோ.
translit: villai malaiyāyk kaikkoṇṭār viṭañcūḻ kaṇṭar viripoḻilcūḻ tillai nakarār oṟṟiyuḷār cērntār allar nāṉavarpāl ollai aṭaintu niṉṟālum uṉṉai aṇaital orupōtum illai eṉilō eṉceykēṉ eṉṉai maṭavār ikaḻārō.
translation: He holds the mountain as a bow. He has a throat ringed with poison. He belongs to the city of Thillai surrounded by wide groves, and he resides in Otriyur. He has not come to me. Even if I swiftly approach him and stand before him, if he tells me he will never embrace me, what will I do? Will not the women mock me?
commentary: The soul speaks as a young woman deeply in love, terrified of being rejected by the Divine. She recalls his immense power, holding the toxic poison of the world in his throat and wielding a whole mountain as a weapon. Knowing his supreme greatness, she worries that if she rushes to him, he might simply refuse her. The mockery of the village women represents the shame of a spiritual seeker who feels abandoned by God.

tamil: திருந்தால் அமர்ந்தார் திருப்புலியூர்ச் சிற்றம் பலத்தில் திருநடம்செய்
மருந்தார் ஒற்றி வாணர்இன்னும் வந்தார் அல்லர் நான்போய்என்
அருந்தாழ் வகல அருள்வீரென் றாலும் ஒன்றும் அறியார்போல்
இருந்தால் அம்மா என்செய்வேன் என்னை மடவார் இகழாரோ.
translit: tiruntāl amarntār tiruppuliyūrc ciṟṟam palattil tirunaṭamcey maruntār oṟṟi vāṇariṉṉum vantār allar nāṉpōyeṉ aruntāḻ vakala aruḷvīreṉ ṟālum oṉṟum aṟiyārpōl iruntāl ammā eṉceyvēṉ eṉṉai maṭavār ikaḻārō.
translation: He sits under the sacred banyan tree. He is the healing nectar who performs the sacred dance in the small hall of holy Puliyur. The Lord of Otriyur still has not come. Even if I go and beg him to grant his grace to remove my deep suffering, if he sits there as if he knows nothing, O mother, what will I do? Will not the women mock me?
commentary: The Lord appears here both as the silent teacher sitting under a banyan tree and as the healing dancer in the sacred hall of Puliyur (another name for Chidambaram). The speaker dreads that he might remain completely untouched by her deep suffering. She fears that pleading with him will do no good if he simply sits in absolute silence, ignoring her pain and leaving her open to public shame.

tamil: அசையா தமர்ந்தும் அண்டமெலாம் அசையப் புலியூர் அம்பலத்தே
நசையா நடிக்கும் நாதர்ஒற்றி நாட்டார் இன்னும் நண்ணிலர்நான்
இசையால் சென்றிங் கென்னைஅணை வீர்என் றுரைப்பேன் எனில்அதற்கும்
இசையார் ஆகில் என்செய்கேன் என்னை மடவார் இகழாரோ.
translit: acaiyā tamarntum aṇṭamelām acaiyap puliyūr ampalattē nacaiyā naṭikkum nātaroṟṟi nāṭṭār iṉṉum naṇṇilarnāṉ icaiyāl ceṉṟiṅ keṉṉai-aṇai vīreṉ ṟuraippēṉ eṉilataṟkum icaiyār ākil eṉceykēṉ eṉṉai maṭavār ikaḻārō.
translation: Though he sits unmoving, he makes all the universes move. He is the Lord who dances joyously in the hall of Puliyur. The Lord of the Otri land has still not approached me. If I approach him with sweet words and say, "Please embrace me here," and he refuses to agree to that, what will I do? Will not the women mock me?
commentary: The poem describes a profound mystery of the Divine: he sits completely still, yet his very presence causes all the universes to move. The soul wonders how to approach such an overwhelming force. She worries that even if she speaks to him with the sweetest, most musical words, he might remain entirely unmoved by her devotion.

tamil: மாற்கா தலிக்கும் மலர்அடியார் மாசற் றிலங்கும் மணிஅனையார்
சேற்கா தலிக்கும் வயல்வளஞ்சூழ் திருவாழ் ஒற்றித் தேவர்அவர்
பாற்கா தலித்துச் சென்றாலும் பாவி அடிநீ யான்அணைதற்
கேற்காய் என்றால் என்செய்வேன் என்னை மடவார் இகழாரோ.
translit: māṟkā talikkum malaraṭiyār mācaṟ ṟilaṅkum maṇi-aṉaiyār cēṟkā talikkum vayalvaḷañcūḻ tiruvāḻ oṟṟit tēvaravar pāṟkā talittuc ceṉṟālum pāvi aṭinī yāṉaṇaitaṟ kēṟkāy eṉṟāl eṉceyvēṉ eṉṉai maṭavār ikaḻārō.
translation: Vishnu deeply loves his lotus feet. He is like a flawless, shining gem. He is the God of divine Otriyur, surrounded by fertile fields where carp love to swim. Even if I go to him with immense love, if he says, "You sinner, you are unfit for my embrace," what will I do? Will not the women mock me?
commentary: The anxiety of the soul deepens into a feeling of complete unworthiness. Great gods like Vishnu worship the Lord's feet with absolute devotion. Comparing herself to that flawless perfection, the speaker fears the Lord will look at her, call her a sinner, and declare her entirely unfit to receive his grace.

tamil: மாழை மலையைச் சிலையாக வளைத்தார் அன்பர் தமைவருத்தும்
ஊழை அழிப்பார் திருஒற்றி ஊரார் இன்னும் உற்றிலர்என்
பாழை அகற்ற நான்செலினும் பாரா திருந்தால் பைங்கொடியே
ஏழை அடிநான் என்செய்வேன் என்னை மடவார் இகழாரோ.
translit: māḻai malaiyaic cilaiyāka vaḷaittār aṉpar tamaivaruttum ūḻai aḻippār tiru-oṟṟi ūrār iṉṉum uṟṟilareṉ pāḻai akaṟṟa nāṉceliṉum pārā tiruntāl paiṅkoṭiyē ēḻai aṭināṉ eṉceyvēṉ eṉṉai maṭavār ikaḻārō.
translation: He bent the golden mountain into a bow. He destroys the karma that torments his devotees. The Lord of holy Otriyur still has not arrived. Even if I go to him to beg him to remove my emptiness, if he refuses to look at me, O vine-like friend, what will this poor woman do? Will not the women mock me?
commentary: The Divine has the power to destroy karma, the accumulated burden of past actions that torments living beings. The speaker desperately wants him to clear away the terrible emptiness inside her. Her greatest fear is not that he lacks the power to help, but that he will simply refuse to look in her direction.

tamil: திடனான் மறையார் திருஒற்றித் தியாகர் அவர்தம் பவனிதனை
மடனா மகன்று காணவந்தால் மலர்க்கை வளைக ளினைக்கவர்ந்து
படனா கணியர் நமைத்திரும்பிப் பாரா தோடு கின்றார்நாம்
உடனா ஓடி னாலும்அவர் ஓட்டம் பிடிக்க ஒண்ணாதே.
translit: tiṭaṉāṉ maṟaiyār tiru-oṟṟit tiyākar avartam pavaṉitaṉai maṭaṉā makaṉṟu kāṇavantāl malarkkai vaḷaika ḷiṉaikkavarntu paṭaṉā kaṇiyar namaittirumpip pārā tōṭu kiṉṟārnām uṭaṉā ōṭi ṉālumavar ōṭṭam piṭikka oṇṇātē.
translation: Lord Thyagar of Otriyur is praised by the firm four Vedas. When we dispel our ignorance and come to see his procession, the Lord wearing the hooded serpent steals the bangles from our flower-like hands. He runs away without turning back to look at us. Even if we run right alongside him, we cannot catch his pace.
commentary: The spiritual journey begins with the soul actively seeking God and stepping out of ignorance to witness his presence. In Tamil love poetry, slipping bangles are a classic sign of a woman pining for her lover. Vallalar uses this image to show how the soul is immediately altered and consumed by divine love the moment it encounters the Lord. Yet God remains fiercely elusive and moves faster than the soul's own efforts can match.

tamil: தக்க வளஞ்சேர் ஒற்றியில்வாழ் தம்பி ரானார் பவனிதனைத்
துக்கம் அகன்று காணவந்தால் துகிலைக் கவர்ந்து துணிவுகொண்டே
பக்க மருவும் நமைத்திரும்பிப் பாரா தோடு கின்றார்நாம்
ஒக்க ஓடி னாலும்அவர் ஓட்டம் பிடிக்க ஒண்ணாதே.
translit: takka vaḷañcēr oṟṟiyilvāḻ tampi rāṉār pavaṉitaṉait tukkam akaṉṟu kāṇavantāl tukilaik kavarntu tuṇivukoṇṭē pakka maruvum namaittirumpip pārā tōṭu kiṉṟārnām okka ōṭi ṉālumavar ōṭṭam piṭikka oṇṇātē.
translation: Our Lord lives in the fittingly fertile city of Otriyur. When we leave our sorrow behind and come to see his procession, he boldly steals our garments. He runs away without turning back to look at us who stand right beside him. Even if we run equally fast, we cannot catch his pace.
commentary: The Lord strips away the worldly protections we use to cover ourselves. Taking the woman's garments symbolizes the soul being stripped of all earthly ego and material identity in the presence of the divine. The soul tries its hardest to keep up with this swift transformation, but human effort alone is never enough to catch God. He takes everything we cling to and still races ahead.

tamil: தாயாய் அளிக்குந் திருஒற்றித் தலத்தார் தமது பவனிதனை
மாயா நலத்தில் காணவந்தால் மருவும் நமது மனங்கவர்ந்து
பாயா விரைவில் நமைத்திரும்பிப் பாரா தோடு கின்றார்நாம்
ஓயா தோடி னாலும்அவர் ஓட்டம் பிடிக்க ஒண்ணாதே.
translit: tāyāy aḷikkun tiru-oṟṟit talattār tamatu pavaṉitaṉai māyā nalattil kāṇavantāl maruvum namatu maṉaṅkavarntu pāyā viraivil namaittirumpip pārā tōṭu kiṉṟārnām ōyā tōṭi ṉālumavar ōṭṭam piṭikka oṇṇātē.
translation: The Lord of Otriyur nurtures us like a mother. When we come in pure goodness to see his procession, he steals our devoted heart. He runs away with bounding speed without turning back to look at us. Even if we run without resting, we cannot catch his pace.
commentary: Vallalar describes God as a nurturing mother who also acts like a thief by stealing the devotee's very heart. This shows that true spiritual love requires a complete surrender of the inner self. Once the heart is given over to the divine, the soul is left breathlessly chasing after God. The mind can no longer rest in the world because its center has been carried away by grace.

tamil: நிலவார் சடையார் திருஒற்றி நிருத்தர் பவனி தனைக்காண
நலவா தரவின் வந்துநின்றால் நங்காய் எனது நாண்கவர்ந்து
பலவா தரவால் நமைத்திரும்பிப் பாரா தோடு கின்றார்நாம்
உலவா தோடி னாலும்அவர் ஓட்டம் பிடிக்க ஒண்ணாதே.
translit: nilavār caṭaiyār tiru-oṟṟi niruttar pavaṉi taṉaikkāṇa nalavā taraviṉ vantuniṉṟāl naṅkāy eṉatu nāṇkavarntu palavā taravāl namaittirumpip pārā tōṭu kiṉṟārnām ulavā tōṭi ṉālumavar ōṭṭam piṭikka oṇṇātē.
translation: The dancing Lord of Otriyur wears the crescent moon in his matted hair. When we come and stand with good desire to see his procession, O friend, he steals my modesty. Despite our many desires, he runs away without turning back to look at us. Even if we run relentlessly, we cannot catch his pace.
commentary: The soul loses its fear of social judgment when confronted by the overwhelming beauty of God. Modesty here represents the boundaries of conventional behavior and the desire to look acceptable to society. The dancing Lord shatters these boundaries completely, leaving the soul exposed and longing. No matter how fiercely the devotee chases after this experience, the ultimate union remains entirely under God's control.

tamil: நாடார் வளங்கொள் ஒற்றிநகர் நாதர் பவனி தனைக்காண
நீடா சையினால் வந்துவந்து நின்றால் நமது நிறைகவர்ந்து
பாடார் வலராம் நமைத்திரும்பிப் பாரா தோடு கின்றார்நாம்
ஓடா தோடி னாலும்அவர் ஓட்டம் பிடிக்க ஒண்ணாதே.
translit: nāṭār vaḷaṅkoḷ oṟṟinakar nātar pavaṉi taṉaikkāṇa nīṭā caiyiṉāl vantuvantu niṉṟāl namatu niṟaikavarntu pāṭār valarām namaittirumpip pārā tōṭu kiṉṟārnām ōṭā tōṭi ṉālumavar ōṭṭam piṭikka oṇṇātē.
translation: The Lord resides in the city of Otriyur with abundant wealth sought by all. When we come again and again and stand with deep longing to see his procession, he steals our chastity. Though we stand strong singing his praise, he runs away without turning back to look at us. Even if we run unceasingly, we cannot catch his pace.
commentary: The deepest longing for God ultimately dissolves our final defenses and self-control. In the language of ancient love poetry, stealing the heroine's chastity represents the total, irreversible capture of her deepest self. The soul sings and stands firm, but God takes away everything that anchors it to the ordinary world. Vallalar shows that divine love is a consuming force that we can never command, only surrender to as it runs endlessly ahead of us.

tamil: அழியா வளத்தார் திருஒற்றி ஐயர் பவனி தனைக்காண
இழியா மகிழ்வி னொடும்வந்தால் என்னே பெண்ணே எழில்கவர்ந்து
பழியா எழிலின் நமைத்திரும்பிப் பாரா தோடு கின்றார்நாம்
ஒழியா தோடி னாலும்அவர் ஓட்டம் பிடிக்க ஒண்ணாதே.
translit: aḻiyā vaḷattār tiru-oṟṟi aiyar pavaṉi taṉaikkāṇa iḻiyā makiḻvi ṉoṭumvantāl eṉṉē peṇṇē eḻilkavarntu paḻiyā eḻiliṉ namaittirumpip pārā tōṭu kiṉṟārnām oḻiyā tōṭi ṉālumavar ōṭṭam piṭikka oṇṇātē.
translation: O friend, I came with unceasing joy to see the procession of the Lord of sacred Otriyur who possesses imperishable wealth. What is this! He stole my beauty and runs away without looking back at us of blameless beauty. Even if we run without stopping, we cannot catch his pace.
commentary: The speaker comes out to watch the temple procession with great joy, but the sight of the Lord takes a sudden toll on her. In Tamil poetry, a young woman falling in love with the passing deity often loses her physical beauty or grows pale from longing. The Lord steals her charm and speeds away, leaving her captivated and entirely unable to catch up with him.

tamil: திரையார் ஓதை ஒற்றியில்வாழ் தியாக ரவர்தம் பவனிதனைக்
கரையா மகிழ்விற் காணவந்தால் கற்பின் நலத்தைக் கவர்ந்துகொண்டு
பரையா தரிக்க நமைத்திரும்பிப் பாரா தோடு கின்றார்நாம்
உரையா தோடி னாலும்அவர் ஓட்டம் பிடிக்க ஒண்ணாதே.
translit: tiraiyār ōtai oṟṟiyilvāḻ tiyāka ravartam pavaṉitaṉaik karaiyā makiḻviṟ kāṇavantāl kaṟpiṉ nalattaik kavarntukoṇṭu paraiyā tarikka namaittirumpip pārā tōṭu kiṉṟārnām uraiyā tōṭi ṉālumavar ōṭṭam piṭikka oṇṇātē.
translation: I came with boundless joy to see the procession of Thyagar who dwells in Otriyur amidst roaring waves. He seized the virtue of my chastity and runs away without looking back at us while the supreme goddess supports him. Even if we run in total silence, we cannot catch his pace.
commentary: The Lord steals the speaker's modesty and traditional virtue, supported by the supreme goddess at his side. In the language of devotion, losing one's chastity means abandoning all worldly attachments and social expectations to surrender completely to God. The soul chases after him in total silence, entirely overwhelmed by this sudden theft.

tamil: கடுக்கா தலித்தார் திருஒற்றிக் காளை அவர்தம் பவனிதனை
விடுக்கா மகிழ்விற் காணவந்தால் விரியும் நமது வினைகவர்ந்து
படுக்கா மதிப்பின் நமைத்திரும்பிப் பாரா தோடு கின்றார்நாம்
உடுக்கா தோடி னாலும்அவர் ஓட்டம் பிடிக்க ஒண்ணாதே.
translit: kaṭukkā talittār tiru-oṟṟik kāḷai avartam pavaṉitaṉai viṭukkā makiḻviṟ kāṇavantāl viriyum namatu viṉaikavarntu paṭukkā matippiṉ namaittirumpip pārā tōṭu kiṉṟārnām uṭukkā tōṭi ṉālumavar ōṭṭam piṭikka oṇṇātē.
translation: I came with unyielding joy to see the procession of the youthful Lord of sacred Otriyur who loves the konrai flowers. He stole our expanding karma and runs away without looking back at us of undiminished worth. Even if we run without putting on our clothes, we cannot catch his pace.
commentary: The nature of the Lord's theft becomes clearly spiritual here. He takes away her accumulating karma, the sum of past actions that binds the soul to the cycle of birth and death. By stealing her karma, he frees her from her deepest burdens, yet he runs away so swiftly that she still cannot reach him. Stripped bare of her past, the soul continues its breathless chase after divine grace.

tamil: தில்லை உடையார் திருஒற்றித் தியாகர் அவர் பவனிதனைக்
கல்லை உருக்கிக் காணவந்தால் கரணம் நமது கரந்திரவி
பல்லை இறுத்தார் நமைத்திரும்பிப் பாரா தோடு கின்றார்நாம்
ஒல்லை ஓடி னாலும்அவர் ஓட்டம் பிடிக்க ஒண்ணாதே.
translit: tillai uṭaiyār tiru-oṟṟit tiyākar avar pavaṉitaṉaik kallai urukkik kāṇavantāl karaṇam namatu karantiravi pallai iṟuttār namaittirumpip pārā tōṭu kiṉṟārnām ollai ōṭi ṉālumavar ōṭṭam piṭikka oṇṇātē.
translation: I came with a heart melting like stone to see the procession of Thyagar of sacred Otriyur who possesses Thillai. He who broke the teeth of the sun stole our inner faculties and runs away without looking back at us. Even if we run swiftly, we cannot catch his pace.
commentary: The Lord now takes the speaker's inner faculties, which are her mind, intellect, and sense of individual self. Without these, she can no longer think or act independently. The verse mentions a traditional story where the Lord broke the teeth of the sun god, showing his absolute supremacy over all other powers. Even with her heart melting and her mind taken from her, the soul learns that it cannot force God to stay.

tamil: மடையார் வாளை வயல்ஒற்றி வள்ளல் பவனி தனைக்காண
அடையா மகிழ்வி னொடும்வந்தால் அம்மா நமது விடயமெலாம்
படையாற் கவர்ந்து நமைத்திரும்பிப் பாரா தோடு கின்றார்நாம்
உடையா தோடி னாலும்அவர் ஓட்டம் பிடிக்க ஒண்ணாதே.
translit: maṭaiyār vāḷai vayaloṟṟi vaḷḷal pavaṉi taṉaikkāṇa aṭaiyā makiḻvi ṉoṭumvantāl ammā namatu viṭayamelām paṭaiyāṟ kavarntu namaittirumpip pārā tōṭu kiṉṟārnām uṭaiyā tōṭi ṉālumavar ōṭṭam piṭikka oṇṇātē.
translation: I came with boundless joy to see the procession of the benefactor of Otriyur surrounded by fields where scabbard fish leap in the sluices. Ah! He forcefully seized all our sensory attachments and runs away without looking back at us. Even if we run without faltering, we cannot catch his pace.
commentary: Finally, the Lord seizes all her sensory attachments, severing her ties to the physical world of sights, sounds, and pleasures. He forcefully takes away everything that distracts the soul. Through this continuous theft of her beauty, virtue, karma, mind, and senses, the Lord strips away every layer of her worldly existence. The soul is left completely bare, running tirelessly after a divine presence that still stays just out of reach.

glossary.def: Aiyaru. A sacred temple town in Tamil Nadu, traditionally called Thiruvaiyaru. Vallalar invokes such holy geography to ground the infinite Lord in approachable local forms.
Alankadu. A sacred temple town famous for the cosmic dance of Siva. Vallalar recites such holy places to emphasize God's vast public glory.
Jains. Vallalar recalls the old stories of the Saiva saints and the Jain monks. In his later songs he says that the Grace Light taught him from the beginning that caste, creed and religion are false.
Anjaikkalam. A historic temple town dedicated to Siva. Vallalar references this shrine to emphasize the universal presence of the divine across various sacred geographies.
Arunai. The holy town of Tiruvannamalai. Vallalar invokes this sacred site to praise the boundless compassion of the Lord who manifests there to melt hearts of stone.
Aruran. An alternate name for the revered saint Sundarar. Vallalar cites God's physical appearance to this saint as proof of divine compassion.
Atikai. An ancient and sacred temple town. Vallalar mentions this holy site to ground his poetry in the rich history of divine miracles, emphasizing that God has always responded to devoted souls.
Jalandhara. A powerful mythological demon destroyed by Siva. Vallalar references this destruction to highlight the supreme cosmic power of the Lord.
Sambandar. A revered child saint of the Saiva tradition. Vallalar references him to highlight the Lord's historic generosity and grace toward true devotees.
Sankara. A title for Siva indicating the giver of peace and joy. Vallalar pairs this name with maternal sweetness to highlight the unconditional care of the divine.

Chidambaram. The sacred temple town, also called Thillai or Puliyur, where Siva performs his cosmic dance. Vallalar uses it to mean both the physical temple and the vast inner space of spiritual consciousness.
Kama. The mythological god of physical desire and romantic love. Vallalar uses the imagery of his fiery flower arrows to symbolize the intense pain the soul feels when separated from God.
Siddhar. A mystic or perfected being. Vallalar applies this term to the divine presence in Otriyur to emphasize God's absolute mastery over all spiritual and mystical forces.
Siva. The supreme God. In his early poetry Vallalar approaches the absolute divine through this traditional form, later expanding this vision into the universal formless Grace-Light.
Jothi. Radiant light. For Vallalar, God is ultimately formless and is worshipped purely as the infinite supreme light, representing the absolute truth and the highest manifestation of divine grace.
Sundarar. A revered ancient Tamil saint. Vallalar recalls how God once acted as a humble messenger for this saint to demonstrate the immense power of true devotion.
Jeevakarunyam. Compassion for all living beings. For Vallalar, this is the mandatory foundation of spiritual life and the only way to receive divine grace.
Ganges. The celestial river. Vallalar mentions the mighty river contained in Siva's matted hair to highlight raw cosmic power.
Kannan, a name of Vishnu (Krishna). In the old story Vishnu became a boar and dug through the earth for ages, yet could not find Siva's feet: God is not reached by effort alone.
Sweet rock candy. Vallalar employs witty wordplay with this term to contrast sweet worldly speech with the hard reality of unyielding stones.
Kavuniyar. The ancient lineage of the child saint Sambandar. Vallalar references him to highlight the Lord's historic generosity and grace toward true devotees.
Kazhumalam. The birthplace of the child saint Sambandar. Vallalar recalls this famous town to connect his own experience of divine beauty with an ancient tradition of absolute devotion.
Murder. Vallalar means the murder of any living being, not only of humans, and condemns it absolutely as a barrier to spiritual life.
The bright yellow konrai blossom sacred to Siva. In these verses it represents the physical token of divine grace that the human soul desperately craves.
Guru. A spiritual teacher or guide. Vallalar emphasizes that the supreme Lord of the universe manifests directly as an intimate, personal teacher to the devoted soul.

Kurava. A traditional mountain community of hunters and fortune-tellers. Vallalar uses the figure of a young Kurava fortune-teller as a literary device to voice the soul's urgent need for reassurance.
A native fragrant flower associated with mountain landscapes and traditional fortune-tellers. Vallalar uses this scent to ground the soul's mystical longing in familiar imagery.
Parvati. The daughter of the mountain. In Vallalar's poetry she represents the divine feminine grace existing as an inseparable half of the Supreme Being.
A young celibate student; here the boy Markandeya, whom the Lord saved from death. True devotion moves God to protect the soul from death itself.
Meru. A massive mythical golden mountain. Vallalar refers to the ancient story of Siva using this mountain as a bow to emphasize the absolute power of the Lord.
Nakkar. The naked one. Vallalar uses this title to describe the Lord's absolute purity, completely unburdened by worldly illusions or material attachments.
Nandi. The sacred bull mount of Siva. Vallalar invokes this traditional symbol to identify the supreme Lord who sometimes remains painfully distant from his devoted follower.
Narayanan. The preserver deity Vishnu. Vallalar includes him to emphasize that the ultimate divine reality encompasses all cosmic forces.

Otriyur, also called Otri: the holy temple town by the sea at the northern edge of Chennai. Vallalar worshipped there in his early years; every poem in this book is set there. The word otri also means a pledge or mortgage, a pun the verses play on.
Pasupati. The supreme Lord of all living beings. Vallalar uses this traditional name to highlight God's role as the compassionate caretaker and ultimate master of every individual soul.
Pandarangar. A specific manifestation of the divine cosmic dancer. Vallalar invokes this dancing form to highlight God's dynamic action in clearing the soul's worldly confusion.
Alms given to a beggar. Vallalar employs it as a pun in these verses, as the word can also mean divine madness.
Brahma. The creator god in Hindu tradition. Vallalar mentions him to show that even the highest orthodox deities cannot easily reach the supreme truth that favors the humble soul.
Indra. The king of the celestial gods. Vallalar lists such powerful rulers to emphasize that true divine intimacy is granted to a longing human heart over mighty cosmic beings.
Base or lowly. Vallalar frequently uses this word to express his own humility and profound sense of unworthiness before God.
Puliyur. Another name for the holy city of Chidambaram. Vallalar invokes this location as the sacred stage where the Divine performs the cosmic dance of grace.
Thillai. The sacred temple town of Chidambaram. Vallalar references this place as the ultimate stage where God performs the cosmic dance of creation and spiritual liberation.
Thirumal. The Tamil name for Vishnu. Vallalar uses this convention to emphasize the absolute, transcendent nature of the ultimate divine reality, which sits beyond the reach of lesser deities.
Thiruvarur. An ancient temple town in Tamil Nadu dedicated to Siva, also known as Arur. Vallalar references this sacred city to invoke God as the supreme giver who grants ultimate spiritual wealth.
Thyagar, Thyagaraja: the great Lord who gives, Siva as worshipped at Otriyur. He is the beloved of every poem in this book.
The bountiful one, who gives without measure. Vallalar uses it for God's boundless giving; his own title, Vallalar, comes from it.
Valli. The indigenous tribal consort of Lord Murugan. Vallalar references her to highlight how the supreme divine actively seeks out humble human souls to offer grace.
Vedas. The ancient sacred scriptures. Vallalar teaches that reciting them cannot replace the direct physical and spiritual experience of God achieved through profound love.
Arjuna. The heroic warrior. Vallalar recalls the myth where Arjuna strikes a disguised Siva with a bow to emphasize that the Lord willingly accepts physical blows to test and bless his followers.
Vidangar. The beautiful Lord. Vallalar uses this name specifically for the presiding deity of Otriyur, highlighting the paradox of a supreme god who deliberately lives as a detached ascetic.
Vishnu. The preserver god in Hindu tradition. Vallalar notes that even great gods like Vishnu praise the Lord to highlight the supreme nature of the ultimate divine light.
